claims.text: AI-generated code volume outruns fixed human review capacity, making code review the bottleneck on shipping software
Reviewer defect-finding effectiveness drops sharply once a single review exceeds a few hundred lines
A change passing its test suite is a weak proxy for whether a maintainer would actually merge it
Running several independent automated review passes and keeping only agreed findings reduces false positives and improves review quality
Automated code reviewers are fooled by confidently framed malicious changes far more often than human reviewers
Teams that stop reading agent-written code accumulate hidden defects that later force large rewrites
Assigning people to review code full time to absorb more volume burns reviewers out
The human role in code review is shifting from reading diffs to designing and tuning the systems that inspect code
Writing tests after the code leaves holes in the suite because hard-to-test code gets skipped
Writing tests first forces the code to be decoupled and testable by construction
A test suite with known gaps gives no decision value when it passes, so it cannot be trusted
Test-first development reduces time spent debugging
Making a failing test pass gives a small reward that makes test-first more enjoyable than writing tests afterwards
A trustworthy automated test suite lets developers change and deploy code without fear
Having the whole team at one keyboard eliminates waiting for answers to blocking questions
Mob programming finishes stories in hours that took individuals working separately weeks
Working as one group on one stream of work removes merge conflicts
Mob programming onboards new members quickly and spreads knowledge so the team does not depend on one person
Switching tasks to fill time while blocked creates work-in-progress inventory instead of fixing the queueing problem
Sustained mob programming requires members to treat each other with kindness, consideration and respect
Pairing or mobbing puts the best of each participant into the code and rarely the worst
Short daily retrospectives keep improvement on track better than infrequent longer ones
Static typing catches type errors at compile time before code reaches users
Static typing yields better runtime performance because the compiler knows each variable's memory layout
Dynamic typing is faster for prototyping and rapid iteration
Static typing suits safety- and performance-critical domains while dynamic typing suits fast-iteration domains
Most software developers, including game developers, work roughly normal hours with only occasional overtime
Crunch is a symptom of poor planning, especially failing to schedule testing and iteration time
Sustained crunch lowers productivity and employee happiness
Much developer overtime is self-imposed from passion rather than mandated by employers
Long-horizon task estimates are inaccurate and managers should not rely on them
Smaller companies tend to have somewhat more overtime than larger ones
Game features need more iteration than business software because feel and fun cannot be specified on paper
Long-lived branches delay integration and produce merge conflicts that grow with team size
Running a CI server is not continuous integration if branches live for days or weeks
Trunk-based development with one small change per release increases release frequency and makes rollbacks easier
Feature flags let unfinished work merge to trunk and decouple deployment from release
Reusing an old feature flag can switch on dormant code paths with catastrophic results
Trunk-based development only works with a fast comprehensive test suite and same-day code review
Ephemeral per-branch environments remove the bottleneck of shared test environments
Trunk-based development is unsuited to products that must tightly control released versions
Developers who deploy their own work to production are happier because they see its impact
Feature flags carry an ongoing removal cost that teams must schedule and pay back
Writing a test per method and mocking every dependency couples tests to implementation so refactoring breaks them
Writing tests slows delivery by a meaningful fraction compared with not writing them
In TDD the unit of isolation is the test, not the class under test
Customer-readable acceptance test suites are rarely read by customers and carry a heavy maintenance burden
Getting a test to green with quick dirty code and then refactoring is faster than engineering the design up front
The refactoring step needs no new tests because behaviour is unchanged and already covered
Tests written to probe implementation details should be deleted once they have served their purpose
Slow UI-driven end-to-end test suites are fragile and break on cosmetic changes
Moving to open-plan offices reduces face-to-face interaction and shifts communication to email and messaging
Open-plan offices increase noise and visual distraction that impairs focused work
Alternating collaboration with individual work produces better solutions than either constant collaboration or isolation
Taking on small third-party dependencies for trivial functions adds fragility out of proportion to the code saved
Coding conventions spread by repetition rather than understanding, producing cargo-cult practices
Comments that restate code are noise and drift out of date because nothing checks them
Work expands to fill the time and headcount given to it
Applying design patterns such as factories everywhere makes code harder to understand than direct code
Names carry most of a program's design intent, so vague names like Manager signal weak design
Logging without stated requirements grows until it dominates the codebase
A single-process monolith is the right default and microservices need a specific justifying outcome
The main benefits of microservices are independent deployability, data isolation and organisational autonomy
Microservices cost more in the short term and rarely save money
Deploying one small service limits the scope and risk of each release compared with redeploying a whole monolith
Coordination cost grows faster than linearly with team count on a shared codebase, which service boundaries contain
Process boundaries enforce modularity that in-process modules fail to because languages let developers violate them
Splitting a shared relational database is the hardest part of decomposition and gives up joins and transactions
Adopting microservices without changing the organisation yields the costs without the benefits
Services that always change together should be merged or re-sliced
Static typing produces fewer bugs and more readable code in large systems
Type inference gives static typing with dynamic-like brevity, removing most of the old verbosity trade-off
DORA metrics measure delivery velocity and stability but do not translate directly into business outcomes
DORA metrics are retrospective and cannot be acted on until after code has shipped
Pull requests spend about half their lifetime idle waiting for someone
Small pull requests are picked up and merged faster
Smaller changes mean less rework, fewer incidents and faster restoration
Developers do not care about DORA metrics, only about merging their code quickly
Automatically approving trivial changes and routing risky ones to senior reviewers speeds flow without losing safety
Line coverage shows code was executed, not that the tests check its behaviour
Mutation score measures test suite quality better than coverage does
A surviving mutant reveals either a missing test or code that can be removed
Mutation testing is too slow to run routinely without parallelisation or incremental selection
Equivalent mutants cannot be detected automatically and require human judgment
Higher-level behavioural tests make mutation testing more practical than many fine-grained unit tests
Full line coverage is relatively easy to reach when a team is motivated
An AI reviewer can take an automated first pass at a pull request before a human reviews it.
Summarizing a change and its risks helps a reviewer understand unfamiliar code faster.
Keeping review feedback, discussion and fixes in one tool removes the context switching that slows review.
Software delivery speed and stability move together rather than trading off; the best teams get both.
Industry and regulatory status do not predict whether DevOps practices improve delivery performance.
Emergency changes made under stress usually skip testing, which is when testing is most needed.
High-performing teams rely on automated test suites and reserve manual effort for exploratory testing.
Infrequent releases leave security patches and compliance updates waiting months to reach production.
Shipping code that has not been exercised by a unit test is unprofessional, and TDD is the surest way to avoid it.
Driving architecture from unit tests without an up-front domain model yields a procedural, bottom-up design that cannot be refactored out of.
Architecture should evolve incrementally, informed by executing code and tests, rather than be designed in full up front.
Some domain structure must be fixed up front because incremental refactoring cannot reach the right architecture from a naive starting point.
Design by contract covers the whole input range of a method, giving broader assurance than sampled unit tests.
Class-level unit tests are hard to trace to business value.
The 10x spread between fastest and slowest programmers is mostly noise: a programmer's own task-to-task variation is as large as the variation between programmers.
Experience, lines of code written and degrees held did not predict programmer productivity.
Productivity differences across programmers follow a long-tailed log-normal distribution, not a bell curve.
Small tasks are easier to estimate and reveal runaway work early enough for the team to intervene.
Shortening sprints too far increases estimation uncertainty because each sprint samples less work.
Hiring super-programmers is a poor route to team productivity compared with improving the working environment.
TDD biases design toward extra abstraction and indirection, which harms clarity unless the designer pushes back.
Unit tests alone cannot catch integration errors, so a suite of only unit tests does not make code self-testing.
The right mix of unit and higher-level tests depends on where a system's complexity lives, not on fixed pyramid ratios.
Higher-level tests often pay back better than unit tests at finding bugs in integration-heavy code.
Estimates become deadlines, and deadlines drive the overtime that destroys sustainable pace.
Hitting an estimate has no value if the software built is the wrong thing.
Story points get converted back into time, defeating their purpose of keeping estimation away from the clock.
Team velocity is mostly set by organizational obstacles, so teams cannot raise it by working harder.
Simply counting completed stories forecasts delivery as accurately as story-point estimation.
Most of a long backlog is wasted because items far down will change before they are reached.
Short fixed-budget increments let the business decide early whether to continue or kill a project, reducing risk without estimates.
Organizations with high software delivery performance are more likely to meet their commercial and non-commercial goals.
Maturity models go out of date too quickly to guide technology transformations.
Technology alone does not raise performance; it must be combined with lean management and organizational culture.
A loosely coupled architecture that lets teams test, deploy and change independently predicts delivery performance more than the platform or technology used.
Lightweight change approval within the team outperforms heavyweight external change approval boards.
A generative, high-trust, blameless organizational culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance.
Transformational leadership is necessary but not sufficient for high delivery performance.
High-performing delivery teams report less deployment pain and burnout and are more likely to recommend their workplace.
Fatigue raises the rate of catastrophic errors, so an overworked team can make net negative progress.
Long working hours raise rates of injury, illness, cardiovascular disease and mental health problems through chronic stress.
Crunch does not improve product outcomes; it correlates with slightly worse ones.
Sleep deprivation impairs cognition like alcohol intoxication and blinds people to their own impairment.
Caffeine tolerance builds within days, so it cannot offset extended overtime.
Letting workers choose their own hours improves satisfaction, health and productivity.
A full day of rest after a missed night of sleep does not restore performance to baseline.
Rewriting a working system from scratch throws away accumulated bug fixes and hands years of lead to competitors.
Code is harder to read than to write, so programmers misjudge old code as a mess.
Architectural problems can be fixed by incremental refactoring without discarding the codebase.
A rewrite team is unlikely to do better because it lacks the original team's experience and repeats old mistakes.
Performance problems concentrate in a small part of a system, so targeted optimization beats a full rewrite.
Dynamic languages became popular because they gave fast feedback and concise syntax for early web work, not because dynamic typing is inherently better.
In-editor type errors give faster feedback than running the program and tracing a crash.
Gradual typing requires a more complex type system and keeps dynamic runtime overhead, so it is not the best of both worlds.
Non-blocking type errors keep the fast feedback of static types without preventing you from running code or tests.
Nearly every mainstream language that emerged after the 2000s is statically typed.
Pull-request review delays feedback and pushes developers to batch changes, making daily integration impossible.
Asynchronous review loses the two-way conversation that makes review educational and lets the author explain intent.
Pull requests were designed to gatekeep untrusted open-source contributors and fit poorly inside a trusted team.
Pair programming provides continuous code review without adding a separate review step that slows delivery.
Most developers who try pair programming end up preferring it.
Pairs sustain focus better than individuals working alone.
Every comment is a failure to express intent in code and should be treated as a necessary evil.
Editors render comments in muted colors, which trains developers to ignore and neglect them.
Complex generic type annotations slow development in statically typed languages on simple algorithmic tasks.
Controlled experiments show statically typed languages have usability advantages over dynamically typed ones.
Static typing forces implementing an entire interface up front even when only part of it is used.
Most software projects run late or over budget, with few finishing early.
The paper that introduced the waterfall diagram warned that the approach was risky and invited failure.
Replacing guesswork with measured experiments is what makes software development an engineering discipline.
Continuous delivery yields order-of-magnitude improvements in quality and efficiency, not incremental gains.
Short cycle times force small teams, automation and fewer handoffs, so continuous delivery drives out lean and agile practices as a side effect.
Automating everything except creative judgment makes releases repeatable and reliable because humans are not.
An automated test is an investment that permanently prevents the class of problem it checks.
Adopting continuous delivery shifts development effort from branch merging and support to new features and lowers cost per product.
A continuous delivery pipeline gives regulated environments end-to-end traceability as a side effect.
Small functions are easier to read and modify but harder to debug, so the evidence for them is mixed.
Abbreviated identifiers are no harder to debug than full-word identifiers.
Code smells mark where bugs are likely, but fixing the smells does not remove the bugs.
Large-scale repository studies claiming some languages produce fewer bugs did not survive replication.
Test-driven development produces no better quality or productivity than other disciplined testing approaches.
Pair programming shows little measurable effect on defects or productivity in controlled studies.
Code review catches most of the defects in reviewed code.
Most code review findings are maintainability improvements rather than functional bugs.
Sleep, stress and hours worked affect output more than any technical practice.
Open-plan offices are adopted mainly because they cut real-estate cost per worker.
How much to invest in tests depends on required feedback frequency, fidelity, overhead and the expected lifespan of the code.
Automated tests give little feedback on whether a feature serves users or whether the codebase is healthy.
Confidence from programmer-written tests led many teams to drop QA and ship lower quality.
Strict TDD, which forbids production code without a failing test, is incompatible with trading off coverage by criticality.
Programmers taking responsibility for quality was a large improvement over throwing code over the wall to QA.
Automating scripted QA checks lets teams get release answers in hours instead of weeks.
Being on call for production teaches developers which tests and feedback loops they are missing.
Agile has been turned from an adjective into a product sold through certification, training and consultancy, losing the original values
No software development rule is universal; every practice only works in a context
Once a developer has internalised test-driven design thinking, the design benefit remains even if the tests are no longer written first
Testing advocacy has become a dogma that shames developers who do not follow it
Scaled agile frameworks appeal to large organisations because they look complex, not because they are shown to work
A good design is one that is easier to change than a bad design, and every design principle follows from that
Agility means taking a small step, evaluating the result and repeating, rather than following a prescribed method
Short certification courses produce practitioners who follow prescribed steps without understanding why
Some programmers are vastly more productive than their typical peers
Rapid individual output often comes at the cost of maintainability that the rest of the team pays for
Most software effort goes into understanding, maintaining, extending and operating code rather than writing it
Excellence in engineering takes different forms; a few well-judged lines can be worth more than high-volume output
A pair finishes a task faster than one person but spends more total person-hours on it
Pairing pays off on novel, hard work and wastes effort on routine or repetitive tasks
Skill mismatch within a pair matters little; every expert and novice combination produces value
Many widely repeated software engineering facts trace back to sources that are missing, measure something else, or are methodologically flawed
The cone of uncertainty in estimation has no empirical basis
Story-point velocity is only stable while the team is stable; adding or removing people changes it
Story points forecast delivery only on average across several iterations, never for a single sprint
Story-point estimation and sprint commitment are alternative ways to fill an iteration, not complements
Automated formatting and static analysis before review let reviewers focus on design and maintainability
Code review is a major channel for learning and knowledge transfer, especially for newcomers
Extensive automated pre-submit checks catch most breaking changes before they are merged
Newly joined engineers receive the most review comments, and the count falls with tenure
Overly harsh or demanding reviews discourage future contributions
Tests serve as precise, unambiguous low-level documentation of the system
GUI-driven integration tests cannot reach a large fraction of code such as error handling and edge cases
Keeping code clean enough to keep development fast is worth more than the cost of building a trustworthy test suite
Focused and collaborative work need different physical spaces
Workspace design is a fundamental part of how a company takes care of its people
The claim that defect fix cost rises exponentially by lifecycle phase has no verifiable measurement behind it
Software project failure rates and crisis figures are exaggerated and often based on opinion surveys
Software folklore spreads because the field is fashion-driven and debunking costs more effort than asserting
Easy-to-repeat claims act as curiosity stoppers that prevent investigating what actually makes projects succeed
Measuring software work in man-months is misleading because adding people does not add proportional progress
Apparent standout productivity can reflect tenure, project selection, information hoarding or credit-taking rather than skill
Version control and code review let junior engineers write production code safely, replacing hierarchical chief-programmer teams
Preferring runtime polymorphism over switch statements makes code slower by forcing pointer indirection and hiding the code path from the compiler
Fusing data layout with the operation in table-driven, data-oriented code can be an order of magnitude faster than encapsulated class hierarchies
Following clean-code structure rules can cost performance equivalent to a decade or more of hardware improvement
The performance penalty of class-hierarchy designs grows as the problem gets more complex
Avoiding repeated code does not conflict with writing fast code
Code organised by operation rather than by type makes shared patterns visible and easier to simplify
Clean-code rules were adopted for maintainability without evidence that they deliver it
Controlled studies find at most small effects of static typing on productivity or defect rates
Differences between individual programmers dwarf differences between languages in experiments
Type annotations help developers mainly by acting as documentation when using unfamiliar APIs
Retrofitting static types onto dynamically typed programs finds only a small fraction of their bugs
Existing type-system studies do not cover experienced programmers, large codebases or modern typed languages
Type-system studies are cherry-picked to confirm whichever side one already holds
Reaching the top few percent in most activities mainly requires correcting basic, observable mistakes rather than talent
Getting feedback on one's own work yields large improvements because almost no practitioners seek any
Tracking where programming time actually goes reveals large, fixable waste that self-perception misses
Skilled coaching beats peer or self feedback for improving at a skill
Independent gut estimates from experienced practitioners converge and are reasonably accurate at project scale
Detailed story-by-story estimation inflates the total because micro-planning is fractal
Estimating individual stories adds little because the biggest risks are cross-cutting unknowns no single story captures
Revealing estimates simultaneously prevents the first number spoken from anchoring the rest
An estimate is better framed as an investment decision than as a contract
Sometimes the honest estimate is that size cannot be known until specific unknowns are investigated
Merge tools cannot detect functional conflicts between independently developed features; only integrating and testing can
Choosing which features to release after integration testing means shipping a combination that was never tested
Trunk-based development with feature toggles is simpler for most teams than disciplined branch-per-feature
Keeping a branch per feature lets a finished feature be pulled before release, which trunk-based development cannot do
Feature toggles are a hack and a source of errors that proper branch-per-feature avoids
Generic repository abstractions over an ORM lead to N+1 queries and joining in application memory
Skipping architecture review in a project's first weeks locks in decisions that take years to undo
Giving requirements without having the engineer explain them back leads to them being silently ignored
AI coding tools reproduce a codebase's existing anti-patterns unless a new pattern is established first
End-to-end browser tests are brittle but the fastest way to get coverage from zero on a legacy system
Writing down architecture decisions and their reasoning helps both humans and AI tools work on a codebase
Reviewing code synchronously at commit time rather than asynchronously reduces merge delay and conflicts
Running the automated test suite before every commit keeps trunk releasable
Trunk-based development requires developers to learn to work in small batches, which many find hard and resist
Programs are rarely inherently I/O bound; chatty serial chains of dependent requests make them look I/O bound
Faster, more responsive software measurably increases user engagement and revenue
Hiding implementation details behind layers of abstraction makes it harder to find why code misbehaves because every layer must be dug through
The readability gains credited to class hierarchies come from cleaning up messy code, which well-named procedural code achieves equally well
Switch-based code is easier to optimise later than a class hierarchy because all cases are visible in one place
Lines of code per feature is a useful objective proxy for code that reads like what it does and stays easy to modify
The 'premature optimisation' quote is misapplied as licence to ignore performance during design when it only warned against early micro-level hand tuning
Developer-time savings claimed from ignoring performance are erased by later ground-up performance rewrites
A performance trade-off only counts as a trade-off if the cost was measured; otherwise it is an excuse
Performance must be designed in from the start because hotspot optimisation cannot fix serial dependency chains and poor data layout later
Decomposing code into very small methods can go too far, producing shallow interfaces and entangled methods that are harder to read than one longer method
Modular decomposition behind simple interfaces reduces the information a programmer must hold in mind at once
Treating comments as failures leads to under-documented code, and missing comments cost far more time than incorrect ones
For most software, conserving programmer time matters more than conserving CPU cycles, so readability-first practices pay off
Choosing the right algorithm improves efficiency by many orders of magnitude while cycle-level tuning gives about one
Clean Code teaching gives performance almost no attention, so its audience learns to ignore it
Interactive and visual behaviour such as GUIs and game feel cannot practically be test-driven because the correct answer is not known up front
Polymorphism makes adding new types easy while switch statements make adding new operations easy; neither is a free win
Dependency inversion via polymorphism protects high-level policy from recompilation and redeployment when low-level details change
Very small changes can be worse than mid-sized ones because their implications are hidden and they are reverted more often
Refactorings should be in separate changes from feature work and bug fixes so reviewers can understand each
Every change that adds or alters logic should ship with its tests in the same change
Almost any large change can be decomposed into a series of small ones by an author who practises it
Very large changes merge faster and are reverted less than mid-sized ones, likely because they are generated or refactor-only
Observed benefits of small PRs are partly selection: teams already practising trunk-based development make smaller PRs
Unit tests that never fail in version control still earn their keep because they fail transiently during development and are fixed before commit
Tests breaking during refactoring is a minor cost in practice
The impossibility of exhaustively testing a program's state space applies to integration tests as much as unit tests
Unit tests make it easy to set up edge-case contexts that are hard to reproduce in the full system
Runtime assertions complement but cannot replace unit tests because an assertion failure is still a production failure
Combining unit and integration tests catches more than integration tests alone
Best practices are inherited from what the most successful programmers do, which cannot distinguish good techniques from bad ones they succeed despite
Making expert advocates argue opposing positions publicly is a partial substitute for missing research
The most damaging software faults are design flaws rather than coding slips
Simple tests of error-handling paths could prevent most catastrophic failures in distributed systems
Lines of code predict defects about as well as any complexity metric
Organisational structure metrics predict defect-prone components better than code metrics
Knowledge-worker productivity cannot be measured reliably, so hours-versus-output conclusions rest on analogies from other industries
Complex mental work degrades faster under fatigue than physical work, so knowledge workers lose more to long hours than manual workers
Managers impose crunch to signal effort rather than because it works
Much delivered functionality is rarely or never used, so working through a prioritised backlog wastes effort compared with selecting high-impact items
Scope growth during a project is mostly value discovered while building, and following the original plan discards it
Estimation techniques were developed for other industries and may not fit software
Technical debt consumes a substantial fraction of developers' working time
Code in unhealthy files has many times more defects and takes several times longer to change than healthy code
Low-quality code makes delivery times unpredictable, not just slower
Technical debt lowers developer happiness and drives attrition
Prioritising refactoring by hotspots, where change frequency meets low code health, targets the debt with the highest interest
Code quality is tolerated as waste because it is invisible to non-technical stakeholders
Splitting services too finely raises inter-service dependencies and coordination so total cost rises again rather than falling
Service boundaries are usually wrong on the first attempt because the domain is not yet understood, so systems built as microservices from scratch tend to end in trouble
Keeping modules in one process with enforced boundaries gets most of the modularity benefit without the distribution cost
Moving functionality across service boundaries is far harder than refactoring inside one process
Headlines about big companies abandoning microservices usually describe one team consolidating a few components
Creating services by which team is free rather than by domain seams produces fragmented systems
Service boundaries must be repartitioned continually as the business changes, so owning microservices is never finished
'Micro' should mean replaceable, not few lines of code
Estimation is a learnable skill: recording estimates and comparing them to outcomes calibrates future estimates
Giving accurate timelines builds trust and is required to advance beyond senior engineering roles
Avoiding estimates improves planning conversations, but business commitments still sometimes require a time-based estimate
Legacy code results from technical neglect, the failure to keep refactoring, rather than from technical debt itself
Automated refactoring tools have existed for decades yet legacy code persists, so the obstacle is mindset not tooling
Never trust a test you have not seen fail
Refactoring in small behaviour-preserving steps with tests or compiler checks at each step avoids the big-bang breakage trap
In refactoring-oriented development most commits reposition code so that the final feature addition is a trivial change
Refactor a problem on its own terms before migrating it to a different paradigm
Programming productivity has no physical ceiling, so hard work can make anyone a 10x engineer
Continuous delivery does not require microservices; monoliths can be deployed continuously
Hype drives teams to adopt microservices they do not need, adding cost and risk
Decomposing a monolith only works if it already has a reasonably modular design; tangled monoliths just produce a mess
Pairing all day is unsustainable because sustained joint focus is exhausting
After-the-fact code review is weaker than pairing because reviewers skim, defer to the author and resist rework already invested
Juniors who always pair can lose confidence and miss learning to solve problems alone
Power dynamics such as seniority or gender distort pairing when one person dominates the keyboard or dismisses suggestions
Pairing limits team work in progress, which improves flow
Pairing's value cannot be proven scientifically because development output is too hard to measure, so teams must try it themselves
Rote, repetitive code is a design smell, and pairing helps find the missing abstraction
Pair programming is an XP practice, not a requirement of agile
Debt is prudent when taken deliberately to ship sooner with small interest, and reckless when taken without understanding its cost
Even excellent teams accumulate inadvertent debt because the right design is only learned by building the system
The debt metaphor helps explain design problems to non-technical stakeholders
Rotating the driver every few minutes keeps every team member engaged
In a mob the group coaches a less-skilled driver on the spot, raising everyone's skills
A rewrite is viable when the codebase is small, the product is not the main revenue source and there is a compelling business case
Rewrite duration grows faster than linearly with codebase size and complexity, making estimates for large rewrites unreliable
Tech debt and distaste for old code alone are not a sufficient reason to rewrite a large successful product
Microservices' independent scaling and fault isolation pay off at very large scale where downtime is costly
No single architecture suits every scale, so architecture should be revisited with each order of magnitude of growth
A single-process design suits long-running compute jobs and predictable traffic better than serverless functions
Microservices speed time to market
Programming needs blocks of at least half a day, so a single mid-block meeting destroys the block
Knowing a block will be interrupted deters starting ambitious work, so a meeting costs more than its duration
Clustering meetings at the end of the day preserves uninterrupted maker time
Managers and makers run on different schedules, and conflict arises when hourly manager slots are imposed on makers
Serverless lets small teams ship without managing infrastructure and often within free tiers
There are no solutions in cloud architecture, only trade-offs
Functions should be extracted until each does one thing, meaning nothing further can be meaningfully extracted
Large functions are classes in disguise; extracting until stuck reveals hidden classes
Function-length rules such as fit on one screen came from historical terminal sizes, not evidence
Story points began as renamed ideal days, meant only to decide how much work fits an iteration
Using story points to predict delivery dates is weak, and comparing teams by velocity or estimate accuracy is harmful
Tracking estimates against actuals shifts attention from delivering value to improving estimates
Slicing stories small enough to finish in about a day gives a smooth flow of value and removes most need for estimates
Frequent small releases deliver more value than big-bang releases whose dates keep receding
Monoliths without enforced boundaries become so coupled that small changes have unexpected effects and newcomers need enormous context
Organising code by business domain rather than technical layer makes code and its owners easier to find
Early in a system's life little design is needed; design investment should start when feature speed begins to slow
Adding public interfaces around modules without untangling the dependency graph just adds indirection and makes code harder to change
Modules can only be reasoned about or tested in isolation when the dependency graph between them is sparse and acyclic
Large architecture changes to an actively developed codebase succeed only by changing average developer behaviour, not by a central team's effort
Imposing uniform coding conventions adds learning and compliance friction without making hard design problems easier
Static dependency analysis gives faster and more actionable boundary enforcement than tracing runtime calls
Large-scale architecture refactors stay in an incomplete intermediate state far longer than planned
Explicit module ownership makes whole-codebase chores like framework upgrades easier to distribute
A small team can maintain a large product across many platforms from a single integrated codebase
Many small services make it easy for knowledge to silo so only one person understands each part
Extracting one slice with divergent performance needs as a separate service captures most of the scaling benefit without distributing the whole system
Many teams that adopted microservices are retreating to monoliths
Measured productivity gaps between programmers are mostly between competent and net-negative developers, not between good and great
Slowing down to investigate a problem before coding reduces later cleanup
Deep expertise in a narrow domain can make an engineer vastly more productive there but less useful elsewhere
Reviewer effectiveness falls off after about an hour of continuous review
Checklists catch omission defects that unstructured review tends to miss
Using code review metrics for performance evaluation makes developers hostile and game the process
Knowing code will be reviewed makes developers write cleaner code even on unreviewed changes
Lightweight tool-assisted review finds as many defects as formal inspection in a fraction of the time
Desirable test properties trade off; making tests more predictive of production makes them slower
Tests that are deterministic and independent of run order are more valuable because flaky results erode trust
A passing test suite should be sufficient evidence that code is ready for production
Static and dynamic typing differ in when types are enforced, not in how many types a language has
Any sound static type system rejects some programs that would never fail at run time
Encoding a dynamically typed program in a static type system bloats it with explicit checks the runtime would do implicitly
Static analysis is unsound and incomplete, so it can augment but not replace a type system
Dynamic languages can run programs that are deliberately not statically type-safe, which helps when exploring or modifying large systems
Unit tests catch most type errors and can give guarantees beyond what static typing provides
Mainstream static type systems cannot express many useful constraints, such as a divisor being non-zero
Small increases in type system expressiveness cause disproportionately large increases in complexity
Type systems themselves contain soundness bugs that are hard to fix without breaking existing programs
Automatic memory management saves a large share of programmer time and removes a class of bugs
Short-lived feature branches with pull requests preserve the benefits of trunk-based development as long as they merge within a day or so
Teams on a shared trunk can scale headcount up or down without losing throughput or quality
Beyond a couple of developers a build server is needed to catch commits that break the trunk
Tools that assign a monetary figure to technical debt produce made-up numbers
Organizations often scale headcount to cope with the mess created by their own neglect rather than to add value
Unmanaged technical debt undermines security because code and dependencies nobody understands cannot be reasoned about
Focusing on one change inevitably leaves side-effect mess that must be cleaned up afterwards
Code does not decay on its own; degradation comes from the changes made to it
Capping pull request size makes developers chain dependent branches instead of working in smaller steps
Working together builds psychological safety better than anything else
Pairing makes waste like slow builds visible and fixed because two people waiting will not tolerate what one accepts
Per-change pull request gates break down under continuous delivery with many deployments a day
Software complexity is whatever makes a system hard to understand and modify, and is judged by its readers rather than its writers
Defining errors out of existence at the interface removes whole classes of error handling
Consistency across a codebase is worth more than any individual better idea that would break it
Productivity being hard to measure does not prevent sound judgments about large differences between people
Relative-size estimation is more accurate than time estimates for complex or uncertain work
Group estimation sessions surface hidden complexity and build shared understanding of the work
Velocity from completed points gives reliable forecasts of future throughput
Time spent estimating is wasted and better spent building
Abstract units shield teams from fixed-deadline pressure and reduce estimate padding
